newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Buoyant markets lift British Airways profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Buoyant markets lift British Airways profits.

text.p: British Airways, lifted by continued strong growth in air travel markets worldwide, on Monday announced record profits and a bumper share-out for staff but warned that the strength of the pound could hit results in the current year.

"Sterling's current strength will adversely impact profits, although it is anticipated that this will at least partially be offset by lower fuel prices and further business efficiency improvement," chairman Sir Colin Marshall said in his results statement.

Pre-tax profits rose 9.4 percent to 640 million pounds ($1 billion) on sales up 7.7 percent at 8.359 billion for the year to March 31, which BA said was achieved despite a surprise jump in oil prices pushing up the fuel bill by 20 percent to 842 million pounds.

The final dividend was increased by a penny to 10.8 pence a share, taking total payout for the year to 15.05 pence, up 10.3 percent, while BA's 58,210 staff are to share 89 millon pounds of profits under a bonus scheme.
The formerly state-owned airline also announced it was giving every employee 10 shares apiece to celebrate its tenth anniversary in the private sector.

Chief executive Robert Ayling declined to say when he expected to see any movement in the complicated approvals process for its tie-up with American Airlines, which had been held up by the British election.
The new Labour government has the task of reviewing the deal in tandem with investigations by the European Union (EU) and the U.S. government.

"I don't expect to hear by any specific date but I think that the momentum is building up again," Ayling told Reuters. "There was inevitably a delay during the period of the election and the authorities here and in Washington and the (EU) Commission in Brussels are all now working again on the case.

"It's a very important deal for us and we are not putting a gun to anyone's head with a particular timetable....We are prepared to be patient about this." BA's results beat market forcasts of between 600 million and 630 million pounds before tax but the share price fell 25 at 735 in a generally lower market after the results.
Traders and analysts said they suspected an element of profit-taking after the shares rallied last week ahead of the results.
"They were very strong before the figures came out -- gaining around 10 percent in recent sessions," said one trader. "You could say, sometimes it is better to travel than to arrive."

Analysts said investors were also betting that BA would eventually win approval for its long-awaited alliance with American. But a degree of caution was likely to limit further gains until there was fresh news.
"Unless something radical happens I would expect the share price to consolidate below the 750 (pence) psychological level and await events," said Nick Cunningham of investment bank BZW.
On the exchange rate issue, Ayling said it was too early to predict whether the greater than expected strength of sterling would be fully offset by other factors in this year's results.
Normally the airline reckons that the affects of currency fluctuations smooth out over time as foreign currency-denominated costs like fuel are involved as well as ticket sales.
The company said the unexpected jump in oil prices added 142 million pounds to its fuel costs last year, and led to a fall of 55 million pounds in operating profits.

BA said it had in the last year already found 600 million pounds of the target billion a year it wants to save through outsourcing and rationalisation. But Ayling warned that it would not be easy to find the remaining 400 million pounds to reach the target by March 2000.
"We have got a long way to go and I don't want people to feel that this is going to be easy," he told Reuters.

Initiatives announced in the last year include a pay-freeze for baggage workers, 400 job cuts in the World Cargo division, rationalisation of some accounting operations, closure of the loss-making Contract Handling business serving third-party airlines at London Heathrow, and outsourcing of ground vehicle services and catering.
The company announced an exceptional charge of 127 million pounds on Monday to cover the redundancy and early retirement costs of these measures.

But this was offset in the headline result by an exceptional gain of 125 million pounds from reversing a 50 percent writeoff made by BA on its 24.6 percent stake in former partner US Airways two years ago.

BA said it was restoring the value of its original $400 million investment in the airline in preparation for the planned sale of its stake. Ayling declined to say when the sale might go ahead, however. ($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
